13: 
14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199: 
200: ---
201: 
202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 3. WHEN TO CREATE REFERENCE FILES
235: 
236: ### Create Reference File When
237: 
238: **Workflow Complexity**:
239: - Multi-phase workflows with validation checkpoints
240: - Decision trees with multiple branches
241: - Pattern libraries with 5+ variations
242: - Systematic debugging procedures
243: 
244: **Technical Depth**:
245: - Root cause analysis required
246: - Tool integration details (MCP, scripts)
247: - Before/after code transformations
248: - Common error patterns and fixes
249: 
250: **Size Threshold**:
251: - Content exceeds 200 lines
252: - Multiple related workflows
253: - Extensive troubleshooting needed
254: 
255: ### Keep in SKILL.md When
256: 
257: **Core Content**:
258: - Overview and "When to Use"
259: - High-level workflow (3-5 steps)
260: - Essential rules (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
261:   > **Note**: RULES sections in SKILL.md use ALL-CAPS H3 headers: `### ALWAYS`, `### NEVER`, `### ESCALATE IF` (or `####` at phase depth). See [skill-md-template.md](./skill-md-template.md) for the complete pattern.
262: - Quick reference
263: 
264: **Size**: Content under 200 lines
265: 
266: ### Reference File Types for AI Agent Skills
267: 
268: | Type                | Purpose                                | Example (kebab-case)          | Size           |
269: | ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------- |
270: | **Workflow**        | Multi-phase processes with checkpoints | `implementation-workflows.md` | 500-1500 lines |

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882:

885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass

1045: ### Directory Purposes

1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines

14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199: 
200: ---
201: 
202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 3. WHEN TO CREATE REFERENCE FILES
235: 
236: ### Create Reference File When
237: 
238: **Workflow Complexity**:
239: - Multi-phase workflows with validation checkpoints
240: - Decision trees with multiple branches
241: - Pattern libraries with 5+ variations
242: - Systematic debugging procedures
243: 
244: **Technical Depth**:
245: - Root cause analysis required
246: - Tool integration details (MCP, scripts)
247: - Before/after code transformations
248: - Common error patterns and fixes
249: 
250: **Size Threshold**:
251: - Content exceeds 200 lines
252: - Multiple related workflows
253: - Extensive troubleshooting needed
254: 
255: ### Keep in SKILL.md When
256: 
257: **Core Content**:
258: - Overview and "When to Use"
259: - High-level workflow (3-5 steps)
260: - Essential rules (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
261:   > **Note**: RULES sections in SKILL.md use ALL-CAPS H3 headers: `### ALWAYS`, `### NEVER`, `### ESCALATE IF` (or `####` at phase depth). See [skill-md-template.md](./skill-md-template.md) for the complete pattern.
262: - Quick reference
263: 
264: **Size**: Content under 200 lines
265: 
266: ### Reference File Types for AI Agent Skills
267: 
268: | Type                | Purpose                                | Example (kebab-case)          | Size           |
269: | ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------- |
270: | **Workflow**        | Multi-phase processes with checkpoints | `implementation-workflows.md` | 500-1500 lines |
271: | **Pattern Library** | Code patterns with before/after        | `shared-patterns.md`          | 300-800 lines  |
272: | **Standards**       | Rules and conventions                  | `code-quality-standards.md`   | 400-1000 lines |
273: | **Debugging**       | Systematic troubleshooting             | `debugging-workflows.md`      | 600-1200 lines |
274: | **Tool Guide**      | MCP/external tool integration          | `devtools-guide.md`           | 200-600 lines  |
275: | **Quick Reference** | Commands, shortcuts, checklists        | `quick-reference.md`          | 200-400 lines  |
276: 
277: **Note:** All authored reference file names use kebab-case (hyphens, lowercase).
278:

281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS
282: 
283: ### Core Principle Statements
284: 
285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom
286: 
287: > **PLACEMENT**: Core Principle goes in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph after the H1 title.
288: 
289: **Format**:
290: ```markdown
291: \## 1. OVERVIEW
292: 
293: ### Purpose
294: 
295: [The outcome this reference produces]
296: 
297: ### When to Use
298: 
299: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
300: 
301: ### Core Principle
302: 
303: [Single powerful statement that captures the workflow's essence]
304: ```
305: 
306: **Examples from Real Skills**:
307: - "Wait for the actual condition you care about, not a guess about how long it takes"
308: - "ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure"
309: - "Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history"
310: 
311: ### Phased Workflows with Validation
312: 
313: **Purpose**: Structured processes with mandatory checkpoints
314: 
315: **Format**:
316: ```markdown
317: ### The [Number] Phases
318: 
319: You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
320: 
321: #### Phase 1: [Phase Name]
322: 
323: **Purpose**: [What this phase accomplishes]
324: 
325: **Actions**:
326: 1. [Action 1]
327: 2. [Action 2]
328: 
329: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`
330: 
331: #### Phase 2: [Phase Name]
332: 
333: [Similar structure]
334: ```
335: 
336: **Key Elements**:
337: - **"You MUST complete"** - Mandatory language
338: - **Named checkpoints** - `checkpoint_name` for validation
339: - **Sequential phases** - Cannot skip ahead
340: 
341: ### Before/After Code Examples
342: 
343: **Purpose**: Show transformation from wrong to right
344: 
345: **Format**:
346: ```markdown
347: ### [Pattern Name]
348: 
349: **BEFORE**: [Problem description]
350: \```[language]
351: // Bad code with issues
352: // Showing what NOT to do
353: \```
354: 
355: **AFTER**: [Solution description]
356: \```[language]
357: // Good code with fixes
358: // Showing correct approach
359: \```
360: 
361: **Why better**: [Explanation of improvement]
362: ```
363: 
364: **Key Elements**:
365: - `BEFORE:` marker for the wrong-way code
366: - `AFTER:` marker for the right-way code
367: - Inline comments explaining issues
368: - "Why better" rationale
369: 
370: ### Pattern Comparison Tables
371: 
372: **Purpose**: Compare approaches across scenarios
373: 
374: **Format**:
375: ```markdown
376: ### Common Patterns
377: 
378: | Scenario     | Approach A (Wrong) | Approach B (Right) | Why Better  |
379: | ------------ | ------------------ | ------------------ | ----------- |
380: | [Scenario 1] | [Wrong way]        | [Right way]        | [Rationale] |
381: | [Scenario 2] | [Wrong way]        | [Right way]        | [Rationale] |
382: ```
383: 
384: **Use when**: Multiple scenarios need comparison
385: 
386: ### Decision Logic in Markdown
387: 
388: **Purpose**: Explicit if/then logic for workflow decisions
389: 
390: **Format**:
391: \```markdown
392: ### Decision Logic
393: 
394: \```markdown

396:   → [Action/Path A]

418: │     └─ Expected outcome B

680: ---
681: 
682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882: 
883: ---
884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006:

13: 
14: > Run one command and know, with a number, whether a markdown document is actually ready to publish.
15: 
16: ---
17: 
18: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
19: 
20: | Aspect | What you get |
21: |---|---|
22: | **Use it for** | Auditing, scoring and optionally improving an existing markdown document's structure and voice |
23: | **Invoke with** | "doc quality", "score this document", "DQI", "HVR" (hub routing only; the packet declares no slash command) |

29: ## 2. OVERVIEW
30: 
31: ### Why This Skill Exists
32: 
33: A document either reads well to the person who wrote it or it does not. A self-assessment is not evidence. Without a scoring pass, "looks fine to me" is the only quality bar a README or `SKILL.md` ever clears. A document can then ship with missing frontmatter, a broken section order, a misdetected document type or robotic AI-pattern prose that nobody catches until an operator hits it mid-task. Fixing that blind, by rewriting on instinct, risks changing product claims or policy text that nobody actually asked to touch.
34: 
35: ### When To Use This Skill
36: 
37: Reach for this packet when a document needs to clear a real quality gate before publishing, when a document "feels off" but nobody has run a structural check on it, when someone asks to optimize or rewrite an existing document for AI-friendliness or when a document needs re-validation after another packet finished authoring it. Skip it when the document does not exist yet (that is a creation packet's job) or when the fix is a one-character typo that does not need a scoring pass.
38: 
39: ### What It Does
40: 
41: `create-quality-control` reads a markdown file and runs it through structure extraction to get a Document Quality Index score with its quality band. It classifies what it finds into blocking/warning/recommendation tiers before applying Human Voice Rules on top. The audit is report-only by default: it tells you where the document stands and why. Only when edits are explicitly requested does it touch the file, staying scoped to that one document. It never creates a new artifact. For that, route to the matching creation packet (`create-readme`, `create-skill` and the rest).
42: 
43: ---
44: 
45: ## 3. QUICK START
46: 
47: **Step 1: Invoke it.** Ask for a doc-quality audit, score or validation of a named file and `sk-doc` routes here. Read `SKILL.md` directly for the full contract.
48: 
49: **Step 2: Run the primary workflow.**
50: 
51: ```bash
52: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/extract_structure.py README.md
53: ```
54: 
55: You get a JSON report with the detected document type, structural metrics, checklist results, DQI score and quality band.
56: 
57: **Step 3: Verify before you rely on it.**
58: 
59: ```bash
60: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/validate_document.py README.md --type readme
61: ```
62: 
63: Expected: zero blocking issues before the document counts as ready.
64: 
65: ---
66: 
67: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
68: 
69: 1. Confirm the target file and pick one execution mode: report-only audit (the default), structure validation, content optimization (only when edits are explicitly requested) or a batch snapshot across multiple docs.
70: 2. Run `extract_structure.py` and treat its JSON output as the source of truth for structure, metrics, checklist results and DQI. Never claim a score without reading it.
71: 3. Classify findings in order: blocking structural failures first, then warnings, then recommendations. Only then apply an HVR voice review, since HVR is a pass after structural issues are understood, not a substitute for finding them.
72: 4. Report findings in the fixed shape: document path and type, DQI score and band, filename-case signal, blocking issues, warnings, HVR issues and recommendations.
73: 5. When edits are explicitly requested, audit the current state for weak patterns, map the document against likely developer questions, apply only the transformation patterns the observed gaps call for, edit narrowly without expanding scope, then re-run `validate_document.py` and `extract_structure.py` to confirm the post-edit DQI and checklist state.
74: 
75: ### Key Concept: DQI Is Read, Never Guessed
76: 
77: The DQI score always comes from running `extract_structure.py` against the real file on disk, never from eyeballing the document. For example, a README can look polished and still be missing a required Quick Start section. The extractor still returns a lower DQI and flags the missing section as a blocking issue. That number is what gets reported, not the impression a fast read leaves.
78: 
79: ### Enforcement Fixes
80: 
81: The three structural failures this packet fixes most often are:
82: 
83: - Missing frontmatter.
84: - Sections out of the required order.
85: - A required section that is simply absent.
86: 
87: Each fix follows the same shape:
88: 
89: 1. Identify the gap against the detected document type.
90: 2. Apply the minimal correction rather than a rewrite.
91: 3. Re-run validation and extraction to confirm the fix actually landed.
92: 
93: When the missing content needs source evidence that is not in the workspace, the packet escalates instead of inventing it.

121: ## 7. FAQ
122: 
123: **Q: Why is the audit report-only by default?**
124: 
125: A: An unrequested edit risks changing product claims or policy text without a real decision behind it. Edits happen only when explicitly asked for.
126: 
127: **Q: Why this instead of letting each creation packet validate its own output?**
128: 
129: A: A creation packet validates what it just wrote. `create-quality-control` audits something that already exists, independent of who authored it or when.

12: # create-quality-control
13: 
14: > Run one command and know, with a number, whether a markdown document is actually ready to publish.
15: 
16: ---
17: 
18: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
19: 
20: | Aspect | What you get |
21: |---|---|
22: | **Use it for** | Auditing, scoring and optionally improving an existing markdown document's structure and voice |
23: | **Invoke with** | "doc quality", "score this document", "DQI", "HVR" (hub routing only; the packet declares no slash command) |
24: | **Works on** | Any existing markdown file already in the repo: README, `SKILL.md`, command doc, spec doc, reference |
25: | **Produces** | A DQI score and band with the blocking/warning/recommendation issue list behind it, plus a targeted edit to that one file only when you ask |
26: 
27: ---
28: 
29: ## 2. OVERVIEW
30: 
31: ### Why This Skill Exists
32: 
33: A document either reads well to the person who wrote it or it does not. A self-assessment is not evidence. Without a scoring pass, "looks fine to me" is the only quality bar a README or `SKILL.md` ever clears. A document can then ship with missing frontmatter, a broken section order, a misdetected document type or robotic AI-pattern prose that nobody catches until an operator hits it mid-task. Fixing that blind, by rewriting on instinct, risks changing product claims or policy text that nobody actually asked to touch.
34: 
35: ### When To Use This Skill
36: 
37: Reach for this packet when a document needs to clear a real quality gate before publishing, when a document "feels off" but nobody has run a structural check on it, when someone asks to optimize or rewrite an existing document for AI-friendliness or when a document needs re-validation after another packet finished authoring it. Skip it when the document does not exist yet (that is a creation packet's job) or when the fix is a one-character typo that does not need a scoring pass.
38: 
39: ### What It Does
40: 
41: `create-quality-control` reads a markdown file and runs it through structure extraction to get a Document Quality Index score with its quality band. It classifies what it finds into blocking/warning/recommendation tiers before applying Human Voice Rules on top. The audit is report-only by default: it tells you where the document stands and why. Only when edits are explicitly requested does it touch the file, staying scoped to that one document. It never creates a new artifact. For that, route to the matching creation packet (`create-readme`, `create-skill` and the rest).
42: 
43: ---
44: 
45: ## 3. QUICK START
46: 
47: **Step 1: Invoke it.** Ask for a doc-quality audit, score or validation of a named file and `sk-doc` routes here. Read `SKILL.md` directly for the full contract.
48: 
49: **Step 2: Run the primary workflow.**
50: 
51: ```bash
52: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/extract_structure.py README.md
53: ```
54: 
55: You get a JSON report with the detected document type, structural metrics, checklist results, DQI score and quality band.
56: 
57: **Step 3: Verify before you rely on it.**
58: 
59: ```bash
60: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/validate_document.py README.md --type readme
61: ```
62: 
63: Expected: zero blocking issues before the document counts as ready.
64: 
65: ---
66: 
67: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
68: 
69: 1. Confirm the target file and pick one execution mode: report-only audit (the default), structure validation, content optimization (only when edits are explicitly requested) or a batch snapshot across multiple docs.
70: 2. Run `extract_structure.py` and treat its JSON output as the source of truth for structure, metrics, checklist results and DQI. Never claim a score without reading it.
71: 3. Classify findings in order: blocking structural failures first, then warnings, then recommendations. Only then apply an HVR voice review, since HVR is a pass after structural issues are understood, not a substitute for finding them.
72: 4. Report findings in the fixed shape: document path and type, DQI score and band, filename-case signal, blocking issues, warnings, HVR issues and recommendations.
73: 5. When edits are explicitly requested, audit the current state for weak patterns, map the document against likely developer questions, apply only the transformation patterns the observed gaps call for, edit narrowly without expanding scope, then re-run `validate_document.py` and `extract_structure.py` to confirm the post-edit DQI and checklist state.
74: 
75: ### Key Concept: DQI Is Read, Never Guessed
76: 
77: The DQI score always comes from running `extract_structure.py` against the real file on disk, never from eyeballing the document. For example, a README can look polished and still be missing a required Quick Start section. The extractor still returns a lower DQI and flags the missing section as a blocking issue. That number is what gets reported, not the impression a fast read leaves.
78: 
79: ### Enforcement Fixes
80: 
81: The three structural failures this packet fixes most often are:
82: 
83: - Missing frontmatter.
84: - Sections out of the required order.
85: - A required section that is simply absent.
86: 
87: Each fix follows the same shape:
88: 
89: 1. Identify the gap against the detected document type.
90: 2. Apply the minimal correction rather than a rewrite.
91: 3. Re-run validation and extraction to confirm the fix actually landed.
92: 
93: When the missing content needs source evidence that is not in the workspace, the packet escalates instead of inventing it.
94: 
95: ---
96: 
97: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
98: 
99: ### Related Skills
100: 
101: | Skill | Relationship |
102: |---|---|
103: | `create-readme`, `create-skill`, `create-agent` and the rest of the creation family | Own brand-new artifact creation. `create-quality-control` never originates a new file |
104: | `create-manual-testing-playbook`, `create-benchmark`, `create-feature-catalog` | Validate inline as part of their own authoring workflow. This packet audits something already shipped |
105: | `sk-code` | Owns code review and debugging. This packet is markdown-only |
106: 
107: ---
108: 
109: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
110: 
111: | What you see | Why | Fix |
112: |---|---|---|
113: | A DQI claim with no extraction evidence behind it | The score was estimated instead of read from the tool | Re-run `extract_structure.py` and cite its JSON output |
114: | Validator flags a document-type mismatch | `extract_structure.py` auto-detected the wrong type | Force the type on `validate_document.py --type <type>`. The extractor itself has no `--type` flag |
115: | An edit touched more than the target document | Optimization scope crept into a nearby file | Revert the unrelated changes. Keep edits scoped to the one file unless the user explicitly expanded scope |
116: | HVR issues were flagged while structural blockers are still open | Voice review ran ahead of the structural gate | Fix blocking structural issues first. HVR is a pass that comes after extraction, not a substitute for it |
117: | A batch snapshot run edited files nobody asked to change | Batch mode drifted from summary into unrequested edits | Batch mode only summarizes per-file type and DQI, with top recommendations noted. Edit only the specific files the user names |
118: 
119: ---
120: 
121: ## 7. FAQ
122: 
123: **Q: Why is the audit report-only by default?**
124: 
125: A: An unrequested edit risks changing product claims or policy text without a real decision behind it. Edits happen only when explicitly asked for.
126: 
127: **Q: Why this instead of letting each creation packet validate its own output?**
128: 
129: A: A creation packet validates what it just wrote. `create-quality-control` audits something that already exists, independent of who authored it or when.
130: 
131: **Q: Does it add a table of contents to the documents it touches?**
132: 
133: A: No, never, unless another active project rule explicitly overrides that.
134: 
135: **Q: What happens if the requested optimization would change a product claim or a legal or policy statement?**
136: 
137: A: The packet escalates instead of editing. Product claims and policy text, plus canonical spec decisions, need a human decision, not a quality-pass rewrite.
138:

99:     guarded = _guard_in_skill(relative_path)
100:     if guarded in inventory and guarded not in seen:
101:         load(guarded)
102:         loaded.append(guarded)
103:         seen.add(guarded)
104: 
105: def score_intents(request) -> dict:
106:     text = request.text.lower()
107:     scores = {intent: 0 for intent in INTENT_MODEL}
108:     for intent, cfg in INTENT_MODEL.items():
109:         for kw in cfg["keywords"]:
110:             if kw in text:
111:                 scores[intent] += cfg["weight"]

115:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
116:     loaded, seen = [], set()
117:     scores = score_intents(request)

121:         return {

123:             "needs_disambiguation": True,
124:             "disambiguation_checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST,
125:             "resources": loaded,

131:     for path in sorted(inventory):

100:     if guarded in inventory and guarded not in seen:

102:         loaded.append(guarded)
103:         seen.add(guarded)

105: def score_intents(request) -> dict:
106:     text = request.text.lower()
107:     scores = {intent: 0 for intent in INTENT_MODEL}
108:     for intent, cfg in INTENT_MODEL.items():
109:         for kw in cfg["keywords"]:
110:             if kw in text:
111:                 scores[intent] += cfg["weight"]
112:     return scores

115:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
116:     loaded, seen = [], set()
117:     scores = score_intents(request)
118: 
119:     if max(scores.values() or [0]) < 4:                      # Tier 1: unclear target/mode

121:         return {

123:             "needs_disambiguation": True,

128:     intent = max(scores, key=scores.get)                      # Tier 2: happy path
129:     # Flat resource topology: no references/<key>/ subdirectories. The intent selects the
130:     # workflow step already documented above, not a keyed subtree; load the flat refs that exist.
131:     for path in sorted(inventory):
132:         load_if_available(path, inventory, loaded, seen)
133:     return {"intent": intent, "resources": loaded}

90: 
91: Read the JSON output and capture:
92: - Detected document type.
93: - Metrics such as word count, heading depth and code ratio.
94: - Checklist results.
95: - DQI score and quality band.
96: - Evaluation prompts or questions surfaced by the extractor.
97: - Structural violations, missing sections and format issues.
98: 
99: Never claim a DQI score without running or reading `extract_structure.py` output.
100: 
101: ### Step 3: Interpret Quality Gates
102: 
103: Classify findings before recommending or editing.
104: 
105: Use this order:
106: 1. **Blocking structural failures**: required frontmatter, required sections, invalid markdown structure, broken required format, README delivery blockers.
107: 2. **Warnings**: weak section order, shallow examples, incomplete usage, poor heading hierarchy, ambiguous document type.
108: 3. **Recommendations**: polish, concision, example expansion, duplicate removal, voice cleanup.
109: 
110: For READMEs, run format validation before claiming completion:
111: 
112: ```bash
113: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/validate_document.py <file>
114: ```
115: 
116: For folder or packet checks, run quick validation:
117: 
118: ```bash
119: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/quick_validate.py <path>
120: ```
121: 
122: If validation exits non-zero, fix blocking errors when edits are in scope, then re-run the failing command.
123: 
124: Run the shared authored-name checker for the target path and report its result as a non-scored filename-case conformance signal:
125: 
126: ```bash
127: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/check_authored_name_kebab.py <file>
128: ```
129: 
130: This signal does not change the DQI score or add a DQI component. It reports `PASS`, `FAIL`, or the canon exemption alongside the scored evidence.
131: 
132: ### Step 4: Apply HVR Voice Review
133: 
134: Review the target for Human Voice Rules after structural issues are understood.
135: 
136: Flag only issues that matter:
137: - Overly generic AI phrasing.
138: - Passive, vague or padded language.
139: - Claims without actionable evidence.
140: - Abstract feature lists where examples would help.
141: - Robotic transitions, repeated sentence shapes or unnecessary throat-clearing.
142: 
143: Do not use HVR as a substitute for structural validation. HVR is a content-quality pass after extraction and gate interpretation.
144: 
145: ### Step 5: Report Findings
146: 
147: For report-only, structure-validation or batch modes, produce a concise report with this shape:
148: 
149: ```markdown
150: **Document**
151: - Path: `<file>`
152: - Type: `<detected type>`
153: - Mode: `<report-only|structure validation|batch snapshot>`
154: 
155: **DQI**
156: - Score: `<score>`
157: - Band: `<band>`
158: - Source: `extract_structure.py`
159: 
160: **Filename Case (non-scored)**
161: - Result: `<PASS|FAIL|EXEMPT>`
162: - Source: `check_authored_name_kebab.py`
163: 
164: **Blocking Issues**
165: - `<issue>` or `None`
166: 
167: **Warnings**
168: - `<issue>` or `None`
169: 
170: **HVR Issues**
171: - `<issue>` or `None`
172: 
173: **Recommendations**
174: - `<actionable next step>`
175: ```
176: 
177: For batch snapshot mode:
178: - Extract each requested file.
179: - Summarize per-file type, DQI, blockers and top recommendations.
180: - Do not edit unless the user explicitly requests edits for specific files.
181: 
182: ---
183: 
184: ## 4. CONTENT OPTIMIZATION WORKFLOW
185: 
186: Use this path only when the user explicitly asks to improve the existing document.
187: 
188: ### Step 1: Audit Current State
189: 
190: Before editing, identify:
191: - Question-answering snippets versus API-only snippets.
192: - Import-only snippets with no usage.
193: - Metadata snippets such as licenses, citations, contributor lists or directory trees.
194: - Duplicate or nearly identical examples.
195: - Missing answers to common developer questions.
196: - Code blocks without language tags or complete setup.
197: 
198: ### Step 2: Generate Question Coverage
199: 
200: For developer-facing docs, map the document against 15-20 likely questions. Cover the relevant items:
201: - Installation and setup.
202: - Basic initialization.
203: - Authentication methods.
204: - Primary use cases.
205: - Configuration options.
206: - Error handling.
207: - Advanced features.
208: - Integration examples.
209: - Testing approaches.
210: 
211: Core principle: answer questions, do not merely document APIs. Developers ask "How do I...?", not "What is the signature of...?".
212: 
213: ### Step 3: Choose Targeted Transformation Patterns
214: 
215: Apply only the patterns needed for the observed gaps:
216: 1. **API reference to usage example**: turn signatures and parameter lists into complete examples.
217: 2. **Import-only to complete setup**: combine imports with initialization and first useful call.
218: 3. **Multiple small snippets to one workflow**: merge fragments into one coherent example.
219: 4. **Remove metadata**: delete licenses, citations, directory trees and governance material that does not help the reader act.
220: 5. **Add error handling**: show realistic failures and recovery.
221: 6. **Combine installation and first usage**: never leave installation as a standalone snippet.
222: 7. **Add configuration examples**: show common dev/prod or option variants.
223: 8. **Demonstrate auth patterns**: include OAuth or token flow when auth is central.
224: 9. **Show batch or bulk operations**: add performance-aware examples when relevant.
225: 10. **Add testing examples**: show how to test code using the library or workflow.
226: 11. **Provide advanced use cases**: include complex real-world scenarios when core docs are already covered.
227: 12. **Add integration examples**: show popular tools or adjacent systems when useful.
228: 13. **Clarify common pitfalls**: show correct and incorrect usage when mistakes are likely.
229: 14. **Add output examples**: show expected result shape.
230: 15. **Consolidate duplicates**: keep one stronger example instead of repeated weak ones.
231: 16. **Fix formatting**: add language tags, valid syntax, necessary imports and consistent naming.
232: 
233: ### Step 4: Prioritize README Improvements
234: 
235: For README-style docs, prioritize:
236: 1. Quick Start: installation plus first usage.
237: 2. Common Use Cases: each major feature with a complete example.
238: 3. Error Handling: realistic failure scenarios.
239: 4. Configuration: common settings and environment differences.
240: 5. Advanced Features: complex but practical workflows.
241: 6. Integration Examples: popular ecosystem integrations.
242: 7. Testing: how to test the documented usage.
243: 8. API Reference: keep only when paired with usage examples.
244: 
245: Minimize or remove:
246: - Installation-only snippets.
247: - Long feature lists.
248: - Project governance.
249: - Licensing text.
250: - Directory trees unless essential.
251: - Academic citations.
252: 
253: ### Step 5: Edit Narrowly
254: 
255: When edits are in scope:
256: 1. Modify only the target document unless the user explicitly expands scope.
257: 2. Preserve correct existing content.
258: 3. Replace weak sections with actionable examples instead of wholesale rewriting.
259: 4. Do not change product claims, policy text, legal text or canonical spec decisions without escalation.
260: 5. Do not create new artifacts from this packet.
261: 
262: ### Step 6: Re-Validate After Edits
263: 
264: After any Write/Edit operation on markdown:
265: 1. Run document validation when applicable.
266: 
267: ```bash
268: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/validate_document.py <file>
269: ```
270: 
271: 2. Run quick validation for the containing packet or skill directory. `quick_validate.py` takes a directory and reads its `SKILL.md`; it errors on a file path.
272: 
273: ```bash
274: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/quick_validate.py <path>
275: ```
276: 
277: 3. Re-run extraction.
278: 
279: ```bash
280: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/extract_structure.py <file>
281: ```
282: 
283: 4. Compare pre-edit and post-edit results:
284:    - DQI score and band.
285:    - Checklist failures.
286:    - Structural violations.
287:    - Remaining warnings.
288:    - Remaining HVR issues.
289: 
290: Do not claim readiness until validation has been run and its result has been read.
291: 
292: ---
293: 
294: ## 5. ENFORCEMENT FIXES
295: 
296: When validation identifies common structural failures, apply these fixes only if edits are in scope.
297: 
298: ### Missing Frontmatter
299: 
300: Detection: SKILL or command file does not start with `---`.
301: 
302: Fix:
303: 1. Determine document type.
304: 2. Ask for missing metadata if it cannot be inferred safely.
305: 3. Insert the correct frontmatter at line 1.
306: 4. Re-run validation and extraction.
307: 
308: ### Incorrect Section Order
309: 
310: Detection: required sections are present but out of sequence.
311: 
312: Fix:
313: 1. Identify current section order.
314: 2. Map it to the required order for the detected document type.
315: 3. Reorder sections without changing meaning.
316: 4. Re-run validation and extraction.
317: 
318: ### Missing Required Sections
319: 
320: Detection: a required section is absent.
321: 
322: Fix:
323: 1. Identify missing sections.
324: 2. Add the minimal required section at the correct position.
325: 3. Fill only content supported by the document or user request.
326: 4. Re-run validation and extraction.
327: 
328: Escalate instead of guessing when required content needs source evidence that is not present.
329: 
330: ---
331: 
332: ## 6. RULES
333: 
334: ### ✅ ALWAYS
335: 
336: 1. Read the target document before judging or editing it.
337: 2. Treat a doc-quality request as report-only unless the user explicitly asks for edits.
338: 3. Use `.skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/extract_structure.py` as the source of truth for structure, metrics, checklist results and DQI.
339: 4. Use validation output to distinguish blockers, warnings and recommendations.
340: 5. Apply HVR voice review before final output.
341: 6. Validate edited documents with `.skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/validate_document.py` when applicable.
342: 7. Re-run `extract_structure.py` after edits to confirm the DQI and checklist state.
343: 8. Keep optimization scoped to the existing target document unless the user expands scope.
344: 9. Report residual risks when the document remains below the requested quality bar.
345: 
346: ### ⛔ NEVER
347: 
348: 1. Never create a new artifact from this packet. Route creation work to the relevant `sk-doc` workflow packet.
349: 2. Never add a packet-local `graph-metadata.json`.
350: 3. Never overwrite original content wholesale when targeted edits solve the issue.
351: 4. Never claim a DQI score without extraction evidence.
352: 5. Never treat HVR as a substitute for structural validation.
353: 6. Never add a table of contents unless another active project rule explicitly overrides the shared standard.
354: 7. Never broaden an audit into unrelated cleanup across nearby docs.
355: 8. Never fabricate examples, claims, commands or source evidence.
356: 
357: ### ⚠️ ESCALATE IF
358: 
359: 1. The document type is ambiguous and `--type` cannot safely resolve it.
360: 2. Validation reports blocking failures that require user decisions.
361: 3. The requested optimization would change product claims, policy text, legal text or canonical spec decisions.
362: 4. The document needs new source evidence that is not present in the workspace.
363: 5. The user asks for edits after a report-only audit but scope or target files are unclear.
364: 
365: ---
366: 
367: ## 7. SUCCESS CRITERIA
368: 
369: A successful `create-quality-control` run produces:
370: - Target document type and file path.
371: - Structure extraction result, including DQI score and quality band.
372: - Checklist failures grouped by blocking, warning and recommendation.
373: - HVR voice issues that matter, not cosmetic nitpicks.
374: - A concise optimization plan when edits are requested.
375: - Post-edit validation evidence when the workflow changes the document.
376: - Clear residual risks when the document remains below the requested quality bar.
377: 
378: Edited documents must also satisfy:
379: - Runnable, standalone examples where examples are present.
380: - Language-tagged code fences.
381: - Complete imports and setup when code usage is shown.
382: - Practical question-answering structure.
383: - No unnecessary metadata copied into instructional sections.
384: - No duplicate or near-duplicate examples unless each answers a distinct question.

22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Workflows define the execution patterns and operational modes for the markdown documentation workflow. These workflows orchestrate structure checks, AI-assisted review, and (when desired) content improvement.

26: - **Mode selection** - Four execution modes for different use cases
27: - **Validation workflow** - Post-operation and pre-submission validation patterns
28: - **Phase orchestration** - Sequential or independent phase execution
29: - **Error handling** - Graceful degradation with clear error messages

32: 
33: - Auditing an existing SKILL/README/knowledge doc → Report-only audit
34: - Answering "is this ready to ship" → Structure validation
35: - Improving an existing README → Content optimization
36: - Assessing a whole doc set → Batch snapshot

43: - [diagrams and flowcharts](../../../sk-design/sk-design-diagram/README.md)

18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Workflows define the execution patterns and operational modes for the markdown documentation workflow. These workflows orchestrate structure checks, AI-assisted review, and (when desired) content improvement.
25: 
26: - **Mode selection** - Four execution modes for different use cases
27: - **Validation workflow** - Post-operation and pre-submission validation patterns
28: - **Phase orchestration** - Sequential or independent phase execution
29: - **Error handling** - Graceful degradation with clear error messages
30: 
31: ### When to Use
32: 
33: - Auditing an existing SKILL/README/knowledge doc → Report-only audit
34: - Answering "is this ready to ship" → Structure validation
35: - Improving an existing README → Content optimization
36: - Assessing a whole doc set → Batch snapshot
37: 
38: > **📍 Context**: This is a Level 3 reference file (loaded on-demand). For the complete progressive disclosure architecture, see [skill_creation/overview.md § Skill Structure System](../../sk-create-skill/references/shared/overview.md#3-skill-structure-system).
39: 
40: **Scope Note**: This reference covers create-quality-control runs only. Other documentation workflows are separate packets rather than numbered modes in this reference:
41: 
42: - [skill creation](../../sk-create-skill/references/README.md)
43: - [diagrams and flowcharts](../../../sk-design/sk-design-diagram/README.md)
44: - [READMEs](../../sk-create-readme/references/README.md)
45: - [manual testing playbooks](../../sk-create-manual-testing-playbook/references/README.md)
46: - [feature catalogs](../../sk-create-feature-catalog/references/README.md)
47:

49:

51:

53: 
54: **"Structure first, optimize second, validate always"** - Enforce valid markdown structure before content optimization, then verify quality at every stage.
